title: Subsequences with a Unique Middle Mode II
statement:
Choose a subsequence of length 5 from `nums`, that is, five indices `i0 < i1 < i2 < i3 < i4`; its middle element is `nums[i2]`. The subsequence is good when its middle element is its only mode: among the five chosen values, `nums[i2]` occurs strictly more times than any other value.

Return how many good subsequences there are, modulo `10^9 + 7`. Different sets of indices count as different subsequences even when they hold the same values.
notes:
## Intuition

Fix the middle index `i` with value `x`. A subsequence adds two elements from each side of `i`, and the verdict depends on how many extra copies of `x` it takes:

- two or more: `x` appears at least 3 times, so nothing ties it; always good;
- none: `x` appears once and any other value ties it; never good;
- exactly one: good only when the other three values all differ.

So count every choice, then subtract the bad ones: no extra copy, or one copy beside a repeated value.

## Approach

1. `right` counts every value; `left` starts empty. For a value with `l` copies left and `r` right, five running sums add up C(l, 2), C(r, 2), l·r, l·r² and l²·r.
2. At index `i`, take the middle out of `right` and subtract `x`'s own terms, so the sums cover only other values.
3. `all` counts every choice of two per side; `noCopy` counts those avoiding `x`.
4. One extra copy on the left (`sameLeft` ways) leaves `a` on the left and `b`, `c` on the right. They clash when `b` and `c` match (`otherLeft · rightPairs`) or `a` matches exactly one of them (`otherRight · cross − crossRight`). The right side mirrors this.
5. Add `all − noCopy − clashLeft − clashRight`, move `x` into `left`, add its terms back, and reduce modulo 10^9 + 7 at the end.

## Example 1, step by step

In `[1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]` there is no other value, so the five sums, `otherLeft`, `otherRight`, `noCopy` and both clashes are all 0. Only `all` counts: C(2, 2) · C(3, 2) = 3 at `i = 2` and C(3, 2) · C(2, 2) = 3 at `i = 3`; other indices lack two elements on one side. The total is 6.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): a constant amount of work per index.
- Space: O(d) for the count maps, d being the number of distinct values.

## Pitfalls

- Equal values at different positions make different subsequences.
- One extra copy is not always bad: against three distinct values `x` wins 2 to 1.
- Remove `x`'s own terms first, or its copies look like clashes.
- Exact counts reach about 8·10^22, so use `BigInt` here; in Java or C reduce after each product and add the modulus before reducing a difference.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `x`, `before`, `after` | the middle value and the number of indices on each side |
| `left`, `right` | count of each value before and after `i` |
| `leftPairs`, `rightPairs`, `cross`, `crossRight`, `crossLeft` | the five running sums |
| `sameLeft`, `sameRight` | other copies of `x` on each side |
| `otherLeft`, `otherRight` | elements on each side that are not `x` |
| `all`, `noCopy` | every choice, and choices with no extra `x` |
| `clashLeft`, `clashRight` | one extra `x` with a repeated other value |
| `total` | good subsequences so far |

narration.2: Count in BigInt: at the full constraints the exact counts are far beyond 2^53.
narration.3: pairs(k) is C(k, 2), the number of ways to choose two of k elements.
narration.6: Before any middle is chosen every element sits on the right, so right starts with every count.
narration.13: shift adds (sign 1n) or removes (sign -1n) one value's terms in all five sums.
narration.20: Load the sums with each value's right-side count; the left side is still empty.
narration.23: Try each index as the middle of the subsequence.
narration.25: Copies of x already on the left.
narration.26: Copies of x on the right, not counting the middle itself.
narration.27: Take x's own terms out, so the sums now describe only the other values.
narration.32: Every way to pick two elements on each side of the middle.
narration.33: Choices with no extra copy of x: x appears once, so it can never be the only mode.
narration.34: One extra x on the left: the other three clash when both right picks match, or the left pick matches exactly one of them.
narration.35: The mirror case: one extra x on the right.
narration.36: Whatever is left is good: two or more extra copies, or one copy with three different other values.
narration.37: Move the middle into the left side...
narration.39: ...and add x's updated terms back into the sums.
